title: Callchain latency fingerprinting — lab notes
content:
Purpose and scope:

This is a working lab note for a new lightweight technique we've been calling "callchain latency fingerprinting". The goal: produce compact, repeatable signatures of common response call-paths (service stacks + kernel hotspots) so we can quickly compare canary vs prod and detect behavioral shifts without re-running full allocations/profiling on every alert.

Why this helps:
- Traditional pprof/jeager traces are heavy; during noisy regressions we need a quick triage signal that narrows hypotheses.
- Fingerprints turn a variable-length trace into a fixed signature we can diff and index in a small time-series store.
- We can correlate fingerprint deltas with metric spikes (token p50/p90, kv-cache-miss rate, scheduling wait) to prioritize root causes.

High-level approach (one-page):
1) Instrument: capture sampled stack traces at response-completion boundary (user visible latencies). Include vtable trace -> runtime -> model-kernel boundary markers.
2) Normalize: trim non-deterministic frames (timestamps, random alloc sites), normalize model library symbols to short names (e.g., conv_qkv -> QKV), and collapse noisy runtime frames (epoll_wait loops).
3) Tokenize: convert normalized frames into an ordered vector where each frame maps to a small token id (u16).
4) Hashing: compute two hashes — an order-sensitive rolling hash (for sequence changes) and a multiset hash (order-insensitive; catches additional work regardless of ordering).
5) Emit: store [rolling-hash, multiset-hash, response-latency-bucket, model, seq-length-bin] as a single metric/event.

Data pipeline suggestions:
- Capture agents: eBPF stack-samples (bpftrace sampling at 200Hz), plus a lightweight in-process tracer that emits stack id at request end (C++/Rust shim).
- Store events in Timescale/Prometheus as gauge + labels, or as logs in Loki with structured fields: fh_rolling, fh_multiset, latency_ms, model, route, canary_tag.
- Keep per-minute cardinality limits: if new fingerprints > 1k/min trigger a sampling reduction.

Grafana panels and queries (examples):
- Top fingerprints by p95 latency: promql: topk(20, quantile_over_time(0.95, request_latency_ms{fingerprint_hash="$fh"}[5m]))
- Fingerprint delta heatmap between canary and prod: get counts per hash in two windows, compute ratio externally and show as table panel.
- Correlate fingerprint emergence with kv-cache-miss: increase_rate(kv_cache_miss_total{fingerprint_hash="$fh"}[5m])

Canary comparison flow (fast triage):
1) When canary p99 exceeds baseline by >20% we snapshot the top 50 fingerprints (by count * p95).
2) Diff the rolling-hash sets: look for new hashes or hashes with >2x latency change.
3) If new fingerprints appear, expand to order-insensitive multiset hash to see if it's reordering or new work.
4) For top candidate hashes, grab full traces for 1–5 requests to inspect frames and kernel activity.
5) If fingerprint implicates scheduling or IO frames (e.g., 'io_read', 'nvme_wait'), escalate to infra SRE; if it implicates quantized-kernel frames, escalate to serving-runtime/ops.

Bisect and gating recommendations:
- Use fingerprint equality as a cheap gating test in bisect commits: if a commit introduces a fingerprint with median latency delta >15% and that fingerprint accounts for >2% of traffic, mark the commit suspect.
- Automate a bisect job that runs microbenchmarks against a commit range, captures fingerprints from synthetic workload (varied seq lengths), and compares distributions.

Example CLI snippets (for lab reproducibility):
- Capture in-process sample (C++ shim):
  LD_PRELOAD=./libfingerprint.so ./run_inference_server &
  curl -sS -X POST http://localhost:8080/generate -d '{"prompt":"short"}'
  # shim emits: FP_RHASH=0x9a4b FF_MHASH=0x7c2b latency_ms=42 model=rw1 route=gen

- bpftrace one-liner to sample stacks at response end (sketch):
  bpftrace -e 'profile:200 { @[ustack(30)] = count(); }' -o /tmp/stacks.out

- Convert stack samples to normalized token stream (python sketch):
  cat /tmp/stacks.out | python3 norm_stacks.py --symbol-map symmap.txt | python3 to_fingerprint.py --rolling > fingerprints.ndjson

Heuristics and gotchas:
- Kernel and driver frames will vary with host kernel version; keep a host-symbol normalization map per image.
- Fingerprints are susceptible to inlined frames — use symbol demangling and inline-unwind heuristics to reduce noise.
- Short requests (<=4 tokens generated) have low entropy stack shapes; require larger sample windows to trust a fingerprint.
- Fingerprints should be used for triage prioritization, not as final RCA; always follow up with full trace/profiling.

Signal prioritization matrix (quick):
- Fingerprint new + latency up + high count -> P0 candidate (immediate rollback/canary cutoff).
- Latency up but no fingerprint change -> look at infra signals (network/CPU steal, host contended NIC).
- Fingerprint reorder (multiset changed, rolling unchanged) -> concurrency/control-flow change (scheduler, batching heuristics).

Example hypothesis log entry (use for bisect/phases):
- hypothesis_id: HYP-20250204-01
- observed: canary p95 +35% vs prod; fingerprint F0x7c2b newly appearing with p95=420ms
- hypothesis: new kernel NVME path introduced in quantized GEMM path -> increased IO blocking
- test plan: capture 100 traces, run perf top on host for top F0x7c2b requests, reproduce with 8 and 32 token sequences; rollback candidate commit X.
- verdict: pending (attach perf dumps)

Dashboard housekeeping and retention:
- Fingerprint index retention: keep full hash index for 30 days, aggregate counts to 180 days.
- Keep raw sample traces for 7 days by default; pin traces around incidents to 90 days for post-mortem.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Can we embed lightweight stack tokens into existing rt-span IDs to avoid a second data path? Pros/cons: saves ingestion but increases trace size and sampling noise.
- Best rolling-hash algorithm: currently testing xxhash64 over a gapped polynomial window vs a Murmur-based scheme. Need benchmarks for collision rates on real traces.
- Can we build a quick ML classifier to group similar fingerprints into semantic buckets (e.g., io-bound, kernel-sched, qkv-bound)?

Immediate action items (owners):
- Jae: prototype in-process shim to emit fingerprint header (due 2025-01-24).
- Lina: Grafana table panel for canary vs prod fingerprint counts (due 2025-01-31).
- Ethan: small bisect job that records fingerprint deltas for every commit in a candidate range (due 2025-02-10).

Notes to self (scratch):
- remember to correlate with token path profiling (hotspot per token position) — sometimes a single long tail token creates a fingerprint that only shows at seq>256.
- keep sampling rate adaptive during incidents; we want representative traces but not a storm of unique fingerprints.
